articles.title: Weather on the board today
articles.body:
A dense fog of regional economic anxiety sat over the morning, obscuring the view of where the Rajpoo industrialists had gone. One Anon asked why the demographic produced no top-tier businessmen, only mid-level managers.

The question hung in the air, unanswered, while the rest of the board moved through the mist. A brief drizzle of consumerist critique fell over the Tata vs.

Eve comparison, light but enough to wet the pavement. It cleared quickly, leaving no residue. Meanwhile, a low-pressure system of dietary orthodoxy developed in the south, with meat eaters declared to be modern-day mlecchas.

The wind carried the warning that one must beware of them, a static charge that buzzed without producing lightning. By midday, the Skirmish front had consolidated.

Yadav larpers and Jaat land claimants clashed in a sudden squall of identity politics, with anons fighting as if their lives depended on the outcome.

The FASM server thread offered a dry spell in contrast, with one Anon noting that implementing CLRS algorithms in C was unremarkable. The skepticism settled like fine dust on the hardware, quiet and persistent.

articles.title: The Missing Rajpoo Industrialists
articles.body:
Anon asked why there are no Rajpoo scientists, industrialists, or successful businessmen on any top list. The poster noted that while every other caste has prominent figures in foreign lands, Rajpoo men seem limited to manual labor abroad.

The thread immediately turned to confirm the absence of these specific professional archetypes. One anon agreed with the premise, stating that there are literally no Rajpoo scientists or major industrialists.

The respondent claimed that even in national sports trials, Rajpoo athletes are consistently defeated by Jaats in every discipline.

The same poster argued that Jaats possess more successful big business figures than Rajpoo men do, both at home and among foreign communities. Another anon provided a personal account from Gujarat, where he witnessed wrestling and grappling nationals.

He described a Jaat grappler bending a Rajpoo athlete like a metal sheet during a match. A different respondent offered a defensive explanation, claiming that Rajputs are warriors who own the military and remain feudal lords in northern India.

This anon suggested that the current image of the caste was being ruined by low-status individuals rather than representing the historical warrior class.

The defense was quickly countered by an anon who pointed out that despite owning the military, Rajpoo men have fewer medals per capita compared to Brahmins and Jaats.

Another respondent asked if owning land for agriculture was the intended contribution of the caste to India. The implication was that feudal land ownership did not equate to the industrial or scientific success demanded by the original question.

The thread moved away from historical roles and focused on measurable outcomes in sports and business. A respondent who had seen similar physical dominance in grappling events confirmed the earlier account, noting that such occurrences were frequent.

The tone of the thread remained hostile toward the Rajpoo identity, with one anon labeling the discussion a low IQ thread before dragging it.

Another labeled the entire interaction as total Brahmin supremacy, indicating that the criticism stemmed from a higher-caste perspective rather than a neutral observation of economic data.

The consensus in the replies was that the lack of Rajpoo presence in science and industry was a fact, not a grievance.

articles.title: Tara vs. Eve
articles.body:
Anon posted a bare comparison between Tara clothing and Eve collection, leaving the specific material or context undefined.

The first response came quickly, with one anon labeling the query as "holy gooner" while simultaneously stating a preference for Eve. The accusation suggested the original poster was acting on immediate impulse rather than reasoned analysis.

Another anon interjected to note that Eve is not a Hindu name, introducing a religious identifier into what had been a simple brand or product comparison.

This claim stood alone without further elaboration or defense in the immediate replies. A third respondent dismissed the religious argument and the initial insult, simply stating that Eve is much cuter.

The assessment focused entirely on aesthetics, ignoring the preceding factual dispute and the character attack. Finally, a fourth anon cut through the noise to declare Tara no doubt superior.

This final verdict ended the exchange without reconciling the claims about names, cuteness, or the nature of the original post.

The thread closed with two opposing factions: those who preferred Eve for its perceived charm or lack of specific religious baggage, and those who stood firmly behind Tara.

articles.title: Dietary Caste Wars on Indiachan
articles.body:
An anons declared meat eaters to be modern day mlecchas and warned others to beware of them.

The reply to this claim was not a rebuttal but a hierarchy of acceptable proteins, with one user arguing that high class red meat like mutton was permissible for Hindus while chicken and eggs were mulla slop to be avoided.

The thread quickly devolved into a census of which castes actually ate meat. One poster listed Bengali Brahmins, Deshasthas, Maithilis, Kashmiris, and Punjabis as non-vegetarian, claiming that universal vegetarianism was a psyop by grain surplus populations to establish a monopoly.

Another user pushed back, insisting Rajputs were the only major group that ate meat significantly, noting that OBCs larping as Rajputs had recently increased consumption. A respondent added that Mohyals, Katakayans, and some Saraswats also ate meat, contradicting the Rajput-centric view.

Ideological justifications mixed with personal grievances. One user claimed that if one did not like the Vaishnav sect, one could simply follow Kaula and eat meat as pleased, provided Aghinya was unharmed.

Another dismissed the moralizing of leftist elites who were detached from reality, while drawing a personal line only at cow meat.

One anon admitted to being a vegcuck who was constantly weight mogged by mullas at the gym and decided to meatmaxx to increase his psl rating. The discussion turned to migration and identity.

One user mocked Punjabi migrants as Khatri cucks running from pasmanda fears, stating that native Brahmins were aryanpilled. Another noted that Rajasthani warriors had historically consumed pure red meat, suggesting current vegetarian trends were recent.

One poster joked that since both Aryans and abbos ate meat, the groups were sem2sem, ignoring the map provided in the thread.

A final post recalled an osint claim about a Chamar from Chamarastra larping as a Raju in the area, wondering what became of him.

The thread ended with a user warning that refusing to eat meat would lead to being brutally mogged by mullas and Timmies in life, reinforcing the initial fear-based framing of the OP.

articles.title: Yadav Larpers and Jaat Land Claims
articles.body:
Anon claimed that Padavs, Mulla, and Abbos have larped as Jhaats, noting a user named Jhujhunafag was fighting with desperate intensity. They argued that the board would not be the same after these individuals left.

A respondent disputed the premise, stating that Yadavs have no reason to larp as Jhaats. They asked what a Yadav would gain by pretending to be a Jhat and questioned the quality of their ancestors' farming.

The same anon asserted that Jaats received the majority of their land only after the abolition of the zamindari system, claiming land owned by Rajputs and tilled by Jaats was handed over to them.

The thread then devolved into mutual obscenity. Anons exchanged profanities involving mothers and genitalia, with one calling the other a randpoot while telling them to send a daughter. Another anon remarked that Thakurs only use Jhaats for oral sex.

The exchange ended with a command to tell the Jhaat to shut up.

articles.title: FASM Server and CLRS Skepticism
articles.body:
Anon dismissed the idea of implementing CLRS algorithms in C as unremarkable, directing attention to a fellow poster who wrote a web server in FASM.

That responsive anon confirmed the project is a simple HTML server of roughly 700 lines of code, still findable on /g/, though development has stalled due to lack of time. Other participants debated the utility of such projects.

One Anon argued that advanced work for freshmen involves building apps and understanding networking and threads, while another noted that most programming jobs revolve around web development, which they dislike.

One poster stated they were coding purely for fun, while another warned that the industry future is tough and advised locking in on basics quickly.
